title: The days of creation
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις συμφορήσας ἐν ψιλαῖς ἀποφάσεσι τὰς διαφορὰς τῶν περὶ κόσμου καὶ ἀνθρώπων γενέσεώς τισι τῶν ἀρχαίων εἰρημένας φησὶ τοὺς τὰ ἡμέτερα συγγράμματα λιπόντας Μωϋσέα καὶ τοὺς προφήτας, οὐκ εἰδότας ἥτις ποτέ ἐστιν ἡ τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων φύσις, συνθεῖναι λῆρον βαθύν. εἰ μὲν οὖν εἰρήκει τὸν δοκοῦντα αὐτῷ τρόπον περὶ τοῦ λῆρον εἶναι βαθὺν τὰ θεῖα γράμματα, κἂν ἐπειράθημεν ἀνασκευάσαι τὰς φανείσας ἐκείνῳ πιθανότητας περὶ τοῦ λῆρον αὐτὰ εἶναι βαθύν· νυνὶ δὲ τὸ ὅμοιον ἐκείνῳ πράττοντες καὶ παίζοντες καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀποφανούμεθα ὅτι τίς ποτε ἐστὶν ἡ φύσις τοῦ νοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις λόγου οὐδαμῶς ὁ Κέλσος εἰδὼς λῆρον συνέθηκε βαθὺν, ἀλαζονικῶς αὐτὸν ἐπιγράψας ἀληθῆ λόγον. ἐπεὶ δὲ ὡς σαφῆ καὶ ἀκριβῶς αὐτῷ νενοημένα προφέρει εἰς κατηγορίαν τὰ περὶ τῶν τῆς κοσμοποιΐας ἡμερῶν, ὧν τινὲς μὲν πρὶν φῶς καὶ οὐρανὸν γενέσθαι ἥλιόν τε καὶ σελήνην καὶ ἀστέρας παρεληλύθασι, τινὲς δὲ μετὰ τὴν τούτων γένεσιν, τοῦτο μόνον ἐπισημειωσόμεθα πρὸς αὐτὸν, ὅτι ἆρ᾿ ἔλαθε Μω(??)σέα τὸ προειρηκέναι ἐν ἓξ ἡμέραις συντετελέσθαι τὸν κόσμον δημιουργούμενον, καὶ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιλαθόμενος τούτοις ἐπιφέρει τὸ „αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως ἀνθρώπων, ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν“; ἀλλ᾿ οὐδεμία πιθανότης ἐστὶ μηδὲν νενοηκότα Μωϋσέα εἰρηκέναι μετὰ τὰ περὶ τῶν ἓξ ἡμερῶν τό· „ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν.“ ἐὰν δέ τις νομίζῃ δύνασθαι ταῦτ᾿ ἀναφέρεσθαι ἐπὶ τὸ „ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν,“ ἐπιστησάτω ὅτι πρὸ τοῦ „γενηθήτω φῶς, καὶ ἐγένετο φῶς“ καὶ τοῦ „ἐκάλεσεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ φῶς ἡμέραν“ λέλεκται τό· „ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν.“
pass_a_gloss: Next to these, having heaped together (συμφορέω) in bare declarations (ψιλαὶ ἀποφάσεις) the differences (διαφοραί) of the things said by some of the ancients (ἀρχαῖοι) about the genesis of world and men, he says that those having left (λείπω) our writings (συγγράμματα), Moses and the prophets, not knowing (οἶδα) whatever is the nature (φύσις) of the world and of men, composed (συντίθημι) deep nonsense (λῆρος βαθύς). If then he had said the manner seeming to him about the divine writings being deep nonsense, we would have tried (πειράομαι) to refute (ἀνασκευάζω) the plausibilities (πιθανότητες) that appeared to him about their being deep nonsense; but now doing the like to him and jesting (παίζω) we too will declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) that Celsus, in no way knowing whatever is the nature of the mind/sense (νοῦς) and of the word/reason (λόγος) in the prophets, composed deep nonsense, boastfully (ἀλαζονικῶς) having entitled (ἐπιγράφω) it true word/doctrine (ἀληθὴς λόγος). Since he brings forward (προφέρω) into accusation (κατηγορία), as clear (σαφής) and precisely (ἀκριβῶς) understood (νοέω) by him, the things about the days (ἡμέραι) of the world-making, of which some passed by (παρέρχομαι) before light and heaven came to be and sun and moon and stars, and some after the genesis of these, we will note (ἐπισημειόομαι) this only toward him: whether it escaped (λανθάνω) Moses to have said before that in six days the world being crafted (δημιουργέω) was completed (συντελέω), and forgetting (ἐπιλανθάνομαι) himself he adds (ἐπιφέρω) to these 'this is the book of genesis of men, in which day God made the heaven and the earth'? But there is no plausibility that Moses, having understood nothing, said after the things about the six days 'in which day God made the heaven and the earth'. If anyone thinks these can be referred (ἀναφέρω) to 'in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth', let him attend that before 'let light come to be (γενηθήτω), and light came to be' and 'God called the light day' was said 'in the beginning God made the heaven and the earth'.
pass_b_english: Next, having heaped together in bare assertions the differences in what some of the ancients said about the generation of the world and of human beings, he says that those who left our writings, Moses and the prophets, did not know what the nature of the world and of human beings is, and composed “profound nonsense.” Now if he had said in what way the divine writings seemed to him profound nonsense, we would have tried to overturn the plausible arguments that appeared to him to show that they are profound nonsense. But as things are, we too will do as he does, and jest, and pronounce that Celsus, who knows nothing at all of the nature of the meaning and of the word in the prophets, has composed profound nonsense and boastfully entitled it “True Doctrine.”

And since he brings forward as a charge, as though it were clear and precisely understood by him, the matter of the days of the making of the world, some of which passed before light and heaven, sun and moon and stars came to be, and some after these came to be, we will remark only this to him. Did it escape Moses that he had said earlier that the world’s making was completed in six days, and does he, forgetting himself, add to this: “This is the book of the generation of men, in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 5:1; Genesis 2:4)? But it is not at all plausible that Moses, with no meaning in his mind, said after the account of the six days, “in the day when God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 2:4).

And if anyone thinks that these words can be referred back to “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1), let him notice that “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) was said before “Let there be light, and there was light” (Genesis 1:3) and before “God called the light day” (Genesis 1:5).

choices.choice: Celsus’s charge is reported in indirect speech; only his phrase λῆρος βαθύς (‘profound nonsense’) and his title ἀληθὴς λόγος (‘True Doctrine’) are put in quotation marks. ‘The nature of the meaning and of the word in the prophets’ (ἡ φύσις τοῦ νοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις λόγου) answers Celsus’s ‘nature of the world and of human beings’; νοῦς may also mean ‘mind’, and λόγος may point to the divine Word speaking in the prophets; lowercase ‘word’ keeps it open. The list ‘before light and heaven, sun and moon and stars came to be’ is translated as the Greek stands, though light appears on the first day; Origen does not correct it. The Greek gives this clause as Origen’s description of the matter Celsus charges, with no ‘he says’, so none is supplied. The quotation ‘This is the book of the generation of men, in the day when God made the heaven and the earth’ joins the opening of Genesis 5:1 (Septuagint: ‘This is the book of the generation of men’) with Genesis 2:4b (Septuagint: ‘in the day when God made the heaven and the earth’); the two references are given in the order the words are quoted. Source has the garbled Μω(??)σέα; read Μωϋσέα. Origen’s argument: since the heaven and earth were made ‘in the beginning’ before light was named ‘day’, the ‘day’ of Genesis 2:4 cannot be a day of the six in the plain sense.
Removed the added 'he says' in the clause on the days (ὧν τινὲς μὲν ... παρεληλύθασι has no verb of saying; attribution must follow the Greek)
'the world was completed in six days in the making' -> 'the world's making was completed in six days' (συντετελέσθαι τὸν κόσμον δημιουργούμενον; calque removed)
'and did he forget himself when he adds' -> 'and does he, forgetting himself, add' (ἐπιλαθόμενος ... ἐπιφέρει; tense mismatch fixed)
'after what concerns the six days' -> 'after the account of the six days'
Citation reordered to quotation order (Genesis 5:1; Genesis 2:4); added missing inline citations on the repeated quotations (Genesis 2:4, Genesis 1:1)
Genesis 1:1, 1:3, 1:5, 2:4 and 5:1 checked against the Septuagint; correct
